1The shape of a distribution

Typed note included in the PDF

He’s starting the list of histogram shapes — the standard set in Devore §1.2. “Uniform” is #1, so the rest are almost certainly coming in this order:

  1. Uniform — flat. Every bar roughly the same height. No peak.
  2. Symmetric / bell-shaped (unimodal) — one peak in the middle, both tails mirror each other. This is the one that leads to the normal distribution later.
  3. Skewed right (positively skewed) — pile of data on the left, long tail stretching right.
  4. Skewed left (negatively skewed) — pile on the right, long tail stretching left.
  5. Bimodal / multimodal — two or more distinct peaks, usually means two groups got mixed into one dataset.

He’ll probably also mention gaps and outliers as things you describe alongside shape.

Unimodal

Bimodal

Typed note included in the PDF Aran’s handwritten notes (photo of a notebook page)

(The shape of distribution)

✎ Explanation (added)

A “mode” here means a peak of the histogram, a bar (or group of bars) that is taller than its neighbours on both sides. Count the peaks: one is unimodal, two is bimodal. A uniform distribution has no peak at all because every class is about equally common.

Textbook · Devore — shapes of histograms (unimodal, bimodal, multimodal, symmetric, positively and negatively skewed): §1.2, p. 22, with the smoothed histograms of Figure 1.12 on p. 23.

Trimodal

Multimodal is used frequently when there is more than one peak or hump.

Symmetric

One half looks the mirror image of the other half

✎ Explanation (added)

“Symmetric” and “unimodal” are separate questions. The left picture is symmetric and unimodal; the right one is symmetric and bimodal. To test symmetry, imagine folding the histogram along its centre line: the two halves should land on each other.

Bell shaped

Normally distributed data is bell shaped, but not all bell shaped distributions are normal.

✎ Explanation (added)

A density curve is the smooth outline you get by imagining more and more data in narrower and narrower classes. “Normal” is one specific bell-shaped curve with an exact formula (it comes later in the course). Other curves are symmetric, single-peaked and bell-like without being that exact curve, so “bell shaped” is the looser description.

Textbook · Devore — Devore’s Figure 1.12(a), p. 23, is the symmetric unimodal picture. The normal curve itself is §4.3.

Skewed Distributions

Right skewed or positively skewed.

Left skewed or negatively skewed.

Skewed in the direction of the longer tail

Board sketches, redrawn: for each direction, a smooth curve on top and a histogram of the same shape below it. The boxed sentence sits between the two on the board.

✎ Explanation (added)

The name comes from the tail, not from where the pile of data is. Right skewed: most values are small and a few large values stretch out to the right (incomes, waiting times). Left skewed: most values are large with a few small ones (scores on an easy test). “Positive” and “negative” refer to the direction on the number line that the long tail points.

2Section 1.3 Measures of Center: the mean

Section 1.3   Measures of Center

The mean is the most common measure of center used by the general public.

An average is just a measure of center and there are many types of averages. Generally, when people just say “average”, they mean the mean.

If these dots are of equal mass, to make it balance, we need to place the fulcrum at the mean (at 3).

Some people say the mean chases extreme values.

3The median, parameters and statistics, and the mode

The Median

We will denote the median by writing .   (Sample, but could also compute a population median)

Given a sample of data values, to find the median, start by ordering the list.

If your sample consists of an odd number of data values, the median is the number in the middle of the list.

If there are an even number of data values, the median is the number that is halfway between the two middle numbers (the mean of the two middle numbers)

Example Examples

Roughly speaking, we expect half the data values to be less than the median and half to be larger.

The median of a sample can be used as an estimate for the value that corresponds to the 50th percentile for the population.

✎ Explanation (added)

Where the middle is: with ordered values the median sits at position . For that is position 5. For it is position 5.5, meaning halfway between the 5th and 6th values, . Notice the median of the second list, 9, is not one of the data values. In the widget above, the median stays at 2 no matter how far the largest value is dragged, because moving the largest value does not change which value is in the middle.

Textbook · Devore — sample median: Definition in §1.3, p. 31, with Example 1.15 (pp. 31–32). Figure 1.16 (p. 32) shows how the mean and median compare for skewed and symmetric populations.

Definition Definitions

A population parameter (or parameter) is a value that uses or considers all values from the population when it is computed.

A sample statistic (or statistic) is a value computed using only values from a sample.

Example Questions

① Is a parameter or a statistic?

It is a parameter. Data values from the entire population are used to compute it.

② Is a parameter or a statistic?

It is a statistic. You only use values from a sample when computing it.

✎ Explanation (added)

A memory aid: parameter goes with population, statistic goes with sample. A parameter is one fixed number (usually unknown, because you rarely see the whole population). A statistic changes every time you take a new sample, and it is what you use to estimate the parameter.

Typed note included in the PDF The mode

The mode is the category that appears most often — the one with the tallest bar on a bar chart.

That’s it. Count the frequency of each category, pick the winner.

Why it matters for categorical data

Because it’s the only measure of center that works. Take blood types: A, B, O, AB. You can’t add them up and divide, so no mean. You can’t sort them into a meaningful order, so no median. But you can count, so the mode survives.

Example — eye colours in a class: brown, brown, blue, green, brown, blue. Brown appears 3 times, blue 2, green 1. Mode = brown.

The ordering distinction he’ll probably draw

  • Nominal (no natural order — blood type, colour, brand): mode only.
  • Ordinal (has an order — Likert scales, letter grades, small/medium/large): mode and median both work, since you can rank them.
  • Quantitative: all three available.

Textbook · Devore — categorical data and sample proportions: §1.3, p. 34. The mode appears only in Supplementary Exercise 74, p. 49.

4Section 1.4 Measures of Variability: variance and standard deviation

Section 1.4   Measures of Variability

We want a measure that tells us how tightly clustered or how spread out the data values are around the mean.

Two very common measures of spread are the variance and the standard deviation.

We will use to denote the population variance and to denote the population standard deviation.

As expected,     and   .

  • under : “The square root of the variance is the standard deviation”
  • under : “↑ The square of the standard deviation is the variance.”

Textbook · Devore — §1.4 Measures of Variability starts on p. 36; Figure 1.18 shows three samples with the same centre and different spread.

We will use to denote a sample variance and to denote a sample standard deviation.

Definition Population variance and standard deviation

For a finite population of data values and with mean ,

← we are computing the average of the squared distance between each value and the population mean.

✎ Explanation (added)

Read the formula from the inside out. is how far one value is from the mean (its deviation). Squaring makes every deviation positive and makes big deviations count much more. Adding and dividing by averages them. So the variance is “the typical squared distance from the mean”, in squared units (cm² if the data are in cm). Taking the square root gives the standard deviation, which is back in the original units and can be read as a typical distance from the mean.

Textbook · Devore — population variance σ² and standard deviation σ: §1.4, p. 38.

Note that if all the values are tightly clustered around the population mean , then the variance and the standard deviation will be very small.

If things are spread out and many values are fairly far away from the mean, (or a couple values are very far from the mean), the standard deviation and variance will be large.

  • A sketch of a histogram and the instruction describe the shape: number of peaks, symmetric or skewed, and in which direction.
  • A list of 8 to 10 numbers: find the mean and the median, and say which one is the better measure of center if there is an extreme value, and why.
  • Compute the sample variance and standard deviation of a small data set using the shortcut formula, showing , and , with units.
  • Derive the shortcut formula starting from the definition or from (he flagged this on the board as a possible quiz or exam question).
  • Show that , and use it to explain why the deviations are squared.
  • Decide whether , , or is a parameter or a statistic, with a one-line reason.
  • Given and , find the outlier limits and say which data values are outliers.
